items.answer: Virtual reality (VR) is an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli provided by a computer, in which a person's actions partially determine what happens and which replaces the user's sense of reality without requiring the physical existence of objects or places.

Presence is a subjective psychological state in which an experience generated by human-made technology is perceived as real, because the user fails to acknowledge the technology's role and perceives computer-generated stimuli as coming from the real world.
Visual sense is a human sense that has electromagnetic energy as its stimulus, photoreceptors as its receptors, and the eye as its sense organ.

Virtual environment is a non-real, computer-generated graphical representation of a real or imaginary world, populated with artificial objects, that is experienced through computer-generated sensory stimuli.

An immersive experience is a perceived experience through sensory organs that appears real, because a person cannot distinguish the experienced environment from their real environment and perceives it as that real environment.

questions.question: Why is audio combined with vision in an immersive XR experience?
options: To replace visual information with a separate audio-only experience
To reduce the number of senses needed for a believable experience
To turn a virtual environment into a physical surround environment
To add sensory information that vision alone may not fully provide
questions.explanation: Vision alone may not give a full picture of the surroundings, so adding audio helps create a more complete immersive experience. It is not meant to replace vision or to reduce the number of senses involved.

questions.question: What does combining audio with visual effects do in a virtual environment?
options: It can reduce the perceived size, volume, material, intensity, and distance of the environment
It can alter the actual size, volume, material, intensity, and distance of the environment
It can replace the visual cues for size, volume, material, intensity, and distance of the environment
It can reinforce the perceived size, volume, material, intensity, and distance of the environment
questions.explanation: Looking alone gives some idea of these properties, but adding audio reinforces their perception. It does not change the actual scene properties or simply replace visual cues.

questions.question: What does presence in a virtual environment require?
options: A head-mounted display and a surround-sound experience
A cave-like display and a wearable display experience
A high-fidelity audio track and a photorealistic visual experience
A believable experience and an attachment to that experience
questions.explanation: Presence depends on the virtual experience feeling believable and on the user developing attachment to it. Specific displays or high-fidelity hardware may help, but they are not the stated requirements for presence.

questions.question: How can audio recording and reproduction count as a VR experience?
options: It can provide a tactile experience even when other senses are missing
It can provide an immersive experience even when other senses are missing
It can provide a scent experience even when other senses are missing
It can provide a visual experience even when other senses are missing
questions.explanation: Audio recording and reproduction can themselves form a VR experience because an immersive effect can still arise without the other senses. It is an auditory, not visual, tactile, or scent-based, experience.

data.text: Immersive virtual reality aims to include several senses because vision alone may not fully convey the surroundings, and using high-fidelity audio technologies can clearly improve the experience. Audio recording and reproduction can already act as a VR experience, while adding sound to visuals reinforces perception of size, volume, material, intensity, and distance. This auditory support, especially when coupled with vision, makes the virtual environment more believable and builds an emotional connection, helping increase presence, which requires believability and attachment.
points: Audio can clearly improve VR immersion because vision alone is incomplete and high-fidelity audio technologies make that possible.
Audio recording and reproduction can themselves be a VR experience and improve immersion.
Combining sound with vision reinforces perception of virtual environment properties like size, volume, material, intensity, and distance.
Audio makes VR believable, and with vision it builds emotional connection, helping increase presence, which requires believability and attachment.

questions.question: Why does sound fail to propagate through a vacuum?
options: It requires a frequency outside the human audible range to remain inaudible
It requires a material medium for pressure variations to travel
It requires photons to carry its energy through empty space
It requires an eardrum to convert the vibration into a percept
questions.explanation: Sound needs a medium such as air, water, or solid material to carry its vibration and pressure variations, so a vacuum provides no path for it. Light is different because it can propagate without a medium.

questions.question: In a sound wave moving through air, what do the compression and rarefaction extremes represent?
options: The maximum and minimum frequency produced by the sound source
The maximum and minimum displacement measured from the rest position
The maximum and minimum pressure produced by displaced molecules
The maximum and minimum phase angle reached during a cycle
questions.explanation: Compression is the high-pressure extreme and rarefaction is the low-pressure extreme of a sound wave. These extremes describe pressure variation, not frequency, amplitude, or phase directly.

questions.question: What physical change at the eardrum is turned into an auditory experience?
options: A time-varying amplitude from the incoming sound wave
A time-varying phase from the incoming sound wave
A time-varying frequency from the incoming sound wave
A time-varying pressure from the incoming sound wave
questions.explanation: The auditory experience arises because pressure at the eardrum varies over time as the sound wave reaches it. Frequency, phase, and amplitude are properties used to describe that wave, but the eardrum response is described in terms of pressure variation.

questions.question: What does the amplitude of a sound wave describe?
options: The number of pressure maxima reached each second
The starting position of a pressure cycle
The maximum displacement from the wave's mean position
The faintest pressure detectable by the human ear
questions.explanation: Amplitude is the maximum displacement of the wave from its mean or rest position. The number of maxima per second is frequency, the starting position of a cycle is phase, and the faintest detectable pressure is a reference level rather than the amplitude itself.

data.text: Sound is a vibration in a medium that spreads as pressure variations between compression and rarefaction. At the eardrum, pressure changing over time is converted into an auditory experience, and the same pressure-versus-time pattern can be represented as a sound wave. Because sound can be represented as a wave, it is characterized by frequency, amplitude, and phase.
points: Sound is a vibration in a medium, propagating as compression and rarefaction pressure variations, and cannot travel in a vacuum.
Time-varying pressure at the eardrum becomes an auditory experience and is plotted as pressure against time.
Frequency, one sound-wave property, is the number of maxima per second in hertz; humans hear 20 to 20,000 Hz.
Amplitude, a sound-wave property, is maximum displacement from rest, measured in decibels relative to humans' minimum detectable at 1000 Hz.
Phase, the remaining sound-wave property, is the cycle start position, measured from 0 to 360 degrees.

questions.question: What two effects do the receiver part and outer-ear canal have on an incoming sound wave?
options: They boost sound pressure in a frequency range and weaken high-frequency waves
They convert the motion of the eardrum into impulses for the brain
They house the tympanic membrane and transfer its vibration to the three ossicles
They create pressure variations in air and carry them to the brain
questions.explanation: The outer ear boosts sound pressure for a range of frequencies, while its folds also weaken high-frequency waves. The other options describe middle-ear, inner-ear, or general sound-propagation effects.

questions.question: What happens in the middle ear when a sound wave strikes the tympanic membrane?
options: The membrane receives the wave and weakens high-frequency waves in the ear
The membrane vibrates and passes the vibration to three ossicles
The chamber sends the vibration to the brain as a sound wave
The membrane amplifies the wave before it enters the canal
questions.explanation: In the middle ear, the tympanic membrane vibrates and transfers that vibration to the malleus, incus, and stapes. The other options assign outer-ear effects or skip the ossicular step.

questions.question: What is the cochlea's function in the hearing system?
options: It receives the sound wave in the outer canal
It boosts sound pressure for a range of frequencies
It houses the three vibrating bones of the middle ear
It converts sound energy into neural impulses
questions.explanation: The cochlea, located in the inner ear, is the sense organ for hearing and changes sound energy into neural impulses. The other options describe structures or effects of the middle or outer ear.

data.text: The human hearing system converts sound into neural impulses through three connected ear structures. The outer ear receives the sound wave, boosts sound pressure for a frequency range through the canal, and attenuates high-frequency waves; the middle ear then transfers the resulting vibration from the tympanic membrane to the malleus, incus, and stapes. In the inner ear, the cochlea uses connected neurons to convert sound energy into neural impulses carried to the brain.
points: The human hearing system contains the outer ear, the middle ear, and the inner ear.
The outer ear receives sound, boosts sound pressure for a frequency range through its canal, and attenuates high-frequency waves.
The middle ear's tympanic membrane vibrates and transfers that vibration to the malleus, incus, and stapes.
The inner ear's cochlea, the hearing sense organ, converts sound energy into neural impulses that neurons carry to the brain.

items.title: Order the conduction of a sound wave from the outer ear to the middle ear
steps: The outer ear receiver receives the sound wave and sends it into the outer-ear canal.
The outer-ear canal amplifies selected frequencies while its folds attenuate high frequencies.
The sound wave strikes the tympanic membrane, causing it to vibrate.
The vibration is transferred to the malleus, incus, and stapes.

questions.question: Why is the auditory component important for presence in a virtual environment?
questions.reference_answer: Presence in a virtual environment requires the virtual experience to be reinforced as believable and attachment to be developed. Audio reinforces the virtual experience as believable, and the auditory experience plays a very important role in increasing presence.

questions.question: How does the outer ear modify a sound wave before it reaches the tympanic membrane?
questions.reference_answer: The receiver part receives the sound wave and forces it to propagate through the outer-ear canal. The canal works as an amplifier by boosting sound pressure for a range of frequencies, while complex folds in the receiver part and outer-ear canal attenuate high-frequency sound waves.

questions.question: How does the fact that sound needs a medium connect to the way a sound wave is represented?
questions.reference_answer: Sound is vibration in a medium, so it requires a medium to propagate. In the medium, sound generation creates pressure variations from a compression extreme to a decompression extreme. A sound wave represents this as pressure variation plotted against time.

questions.question: How do the middle and inner ears transform a sound wave into a signal the brain can use?
questions.reference_answer: In the middle ear, the sound wave strikes the tympanic membrane, causing it to vibrate, and the vibration is transferred to the malleus, incus, and stapes. In the inner ear, the cochlea converts sound energy into neural impulses. Those neural impulses are transmitted to the brain through the neural network.
